title: Split Into Known Words
statement:
You get a string s and a list of dictionary words. Return true if s can be cut into pieces so that every piece is a dictionary word, and false otherwise.

A word may be used any number of times, and not every word has to be used.

examples.why: "tea" + "leaf". Grabbing the longest word first takes "teal" and is left with "eaf", which fails.
"carpet" + "s". Grabbing the shortest word first takes "car" and is stuck on "pets", so neither greedy choice is safe.
"door" + "knob" covers everything but the final "s", and no word ends there.

constraints: s and words[i] hold lowercase English letters
hints: Neither longest-first nor shortest-first works. You need to try every word that fits at a given position, but without redoing work.
Whether the rest of the string can be split depends only on where the rest starts. So there are only n + 1 different questions.

Let ok(i) mean the first i letters can be split. ok(0) = true, and ok(i) is true if some j < i has ok(j) and s[j..i−1] in the dictionary. Put the words in a set and only try piece lengths up to the longest word.

explain.intuition:
A greedy cutter commits to one word and can be wrong either way, as the first two examples show. Plain backtracking tries everything but can repeat the same suffix exponentially often (think of a long run of a with words a, aa, aaa). The fix is to notice that the only thing that matters is where the next piece starts.

State: ok(i) = the prefix s[0..i−1] (first i letters) can be split into words. Recurrence: look at the last piece, s[j..i−1]. The prefix splits exactly when some j has ok(j) true and that piece is a word. Base: ok(0) = true, the empty prefix. Fill i = 1 … n; the answer is ok(n). Words are at most 20 letters, so only j ≥ i − 20 needs checking, and a set makes each lookup fast.
steps: Put the words in a set and note the longest word length maxLen.
State: ok[i] = first i letters can be split. Base: ok[0] = true.
Recurrence: ok[i] = true if some j in [i − maxLen, i − 1] has ok[j] and s.slice(j, i) in the set.
Stop scanning j as soon as one works.
pitfalls: Greedy cutting, longest or shortest first. The first two examples break one each.
Backtracking without a memo. On a long run of a ending in b, with words a, aa, aaa, it explores an exponential number of cuts before answering false.
Forgetting ok[0] = true. Then no first piece can ever be accepted.

complexity.time: O(n · L²) with L = longest word

solutions.title: Backtracking
solutions.idea: At each position try every word that matches there and recurse on the rest. Correct but exponential on repetitive input.

solutions.title: Backtracking with a memo
solutions.idea: Same search, but remember for each start position whether the rest can be split. Each position is solved once.

solutions.title: Table over prefixes
solutions.idea: ok[i] says the first i letters split into words. Check the last piece against a set, only up to the longest word length.

followups: Return every possible split as a list of sentences. Why can the output be exponential, and how does the table help prune?
The dictionary has a million words. Would a trie walk from each reachable position be faster than slicing?
